trap: It turns into a scolding to "be good soil" — as if dirt could improve itself — which is both impossible and tone-deaf to the wild generosity of the sowing. Or it becomes pure reassurance ("the Word never fails") that quietly ignores the three-quarters that bore nothing.
hinge: The seed is flung with abandon on ground that cannot, by itself, change what it is — and still the call is to hear and bear fruit. The Sower's recklessness and the soil's responsibility both stand; drop either and the parable goes flat.

doors.claim: The four soils are a mirror held up to the hearer — the trodden path, the shallow rock, the choking thorns, the open field — and the sermon asks which you are today.

witnesses.author: Rabanus Maurus
witnesses.reading: The wayside is the mind trodden and hardened by the continual passage of evil thoughts, so that the seed cannot sink in.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word, for riches are treacherous — promising one thing and doing another.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: They are sown upon the rock and among thorns who receive well: but either adversity by terrifying, or prosperity by flattering, holds them back from bringing to perfection.

doors.say: The same seed fell on all four grounds; the difference was the soil — and the soil is you.
doors.do: Have each hearer name which ground their heart is this season, and the one thing trodding, drying, or choking the word in them.

doors.claim: No careful farmer sows on a footpath, on rock, in thorns — but this Sower scatters everywhere, and that abandon is the gospel: God writes off no ground.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: How is it reasonable to sow among thorns, on stony ground, by the wayside? In ordinary soil it would be folly — but the Sower casts the seed even there.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: By this Sower is meant the Son of God, who sows among the people the word of the Father.

doors.say: Look how prodigally God spends the seed — on the hardened, the shallow, the crowded — refusing to decide in advance which ground is hopeless.
doors.do: Turn them from writing off a hard "soil" in their life — a person, a place — to scattering the word there anyway.

doors.claim: Good soil is not just receptive but fruitful — it hears, understands, and yields; a faith that takes the word in and grows nothing is not yet the good ground.

witnesses.author: Remigius of Auxerre
witnesses.reading: These ears to hear are the ears of the mind — to understand, and to do the things that are commanded.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The good ground is the one who hears the word and considers it — in spite of Satan; it has deep root, and brings forth fruit in various proportions, some a hundredfold.

doors.say: The test of the word in you is not how warmly you received it but what it has grown.
doors.do: Send them to one concrete fruit the word is asking of them this month — and to tend it, not just admire the seed.

complementary.gravity: Isaiah promises a word that goes out like rain and does not return empty; the Psalm soaks the furrows and crowns the year with bounty; and Jesus flings seed across every kind of ground. The nerve: the Word is already doing its work — the open question is the ground it lands on, and you are the ground.

synthesis.convergence: Three of the readings sing of a Word and Spirit doing fertile, unstoppable work — rain that does not return empty (Isaiah 55), furrows soaked and the year crowned (Psalm 65), the Spirit giving life and freedom (Romans 8) — and the fourth asks only whether that seed finds root in us (the Sower).
synthesis.claim: God's word is already at work and will not come back empty; your part is not to manufacture the harvest but to be ground that lets it root.
synthesis.here: For anxious sowers — parents, teachers, pastors — who fear their labor falls on hard ground, the move is to trust the seed's own power and the Spirit's fertility: keep scattering, and tend the soil of your own attention rather than counting the yield.

doors.claim: Esau despises what was given for what he is hungry for now, and the tragedy is less the bargain than the shrug that follows it.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: He did eat and drink, and rise up and went his way — without any serious reflections upon the ill bargain he had made, or any shew of regret. Thus Esau despised his birth-right.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Lovers of the world cultivate outward things the more, the more they leave their own inward things untilled.

doors.say: He ate, he drank, he got up and left. The saddest thing in the story is how little it seemed to cost him.
doors.do: Ask them to name one small, repeated trade that is spending down something God gave them, and to reverse it once this week.

doors.claim: Isaac keeps praying through two decades of barrenness: the promise does not replace prayer, it is the reason to keep praying.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Though God had promised to multiply his family, he prayed for it; for God's promises must not supersede but encourage our prayers. Though he had prayed for this mercy many years, and it was not granted, yet he did not leave off praying for it.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Think not that he obtained forthwith and at once what he desired: for he continued twenty years praying and beseeching God.

doors.say: The promise was already given, and still Isaac prayed for twenty years. Waiting was not a sign he had been forgotten.
doors.do: Invite them to take up again a prayer they set down because the answer was slow.

doors.claim: The twins' struggle is ours as well: flesh and Spirit contend inside a single life, and Rebekah shows where to take it.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Two nations and two peoples are within us, namely of the vices and of the virtues. Yet the people overcomes the people, and the elder shall serve the younger, namely the flesh the spirit, and the vices the virtues.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: It is a mighty ease to spread our case before the Lord, and ask council at his mouth.

doors.say: There is a struggle going on inside you, and Rebekah did the right thing with hers: she went and asked God about it.
doors.do: Have them name the two things wrestling in them this season and bring both, by name, to prayer.

semicontinuous.gravity: Isaac prays for years before Rebekah conceives; the twins struggle in her womb; and Esau, faint from the field, sells his birthright for a bowl of red stew (Genesis 25). The Psalm calls God's word a lamp to the feet; Paul sets the mind of the flesh against the mind of the Spirit (Romans 8); and Jesus flings seed on every kind of ground. The nerve: what we will trade away for whatever satisfies right now.

synthesis.convergence: Esau trades a birthright for one meal and walks off without regret (Genesis 25); the psalmist keeps God's word as a lamp for the next step (Psalm 119); Paul sets the mind of the flesh against the mind of the Spirit (Romans 8); and in the Sower the word is choked by cares and the lure of riches (Matthew 13). Each reading weighs the gift God gives against the hunger of the moment, and shows how easily the lasting thing is sold for the immediate one.
synthesis.claim: The word God sows is a birthright, not a snack: guard it from the hunger that would sell it for something quicker.
synthesis.here: For people whose attention goes out daily in small bargains — the scroll, the rush, the urgent thing that isn't — the move is to name which is the birthright and which is the stew, and to refuse one trade this week.

subtract: Three doors, three landings — self-examination (which ground), grace (the reckless Sower), fruitfulness (hearing that yields). Walk through one; the choosing is the focus.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
